title: Inheritance & Access Specifiers
html:
A derived class inherits the members of its base class and can add or customise behaviour. Public inheritance models an is-a relationship.

Basics

Order

Construction goes base → members → derived body; destruction runs in exactly the reverse order.

Inheritance access

Base member is…public inheritanceprotected inheritanceprivate inheritance
publicpublicprotectedprivate
protectedprotectedprotectedprivate
privateinaccessibleinaccessibleinaccessible
  • public inheritance = is-a (a Dog can be used wherever an Animal& is expected). 99% of the time this is what you want.
  • private inheritance = implemented-in-terms-of — usually better expressed with composition (a member).
  • class D : B defaults to private inheritance; struct D : B to public.

Hiding, using and calling the base version

Watch out

Declaring a function in the derived class with the same name hides all base overloads of that name, whatever their parameters. Bring them back with using Base::name;.

Composition vs inheritance

Do

Use inheritance for genuine is-a relationships with polymorphic behaviour; prefer composition (has-a) for reuse: a Car has an Engine.

Avoid

Inheriting just to reuse code (class Stack : public std::vector<int>) — it exposes every base operation and couples you to its implementation.

What is not inherited from a base class?

Constructors (unless brought in with using Base::Base;), the destructor, copy/move assignment operators (the derived class gets its own implicitly-declared ones), and friendships. Private members are inherited — they're part of the object — but not accessible.
